--- Page 1 ---
Toward Self-Evolving Geospatial Algorithms: An
LLM-Driven Framework with a Case Study on Spatial
Regime Discovery⋆,⋆⋆
Xiayin Loua, Peng Luob,c,∗, Liqiu Menga
aChair of Cartography and Visual Analytics, Technical University of Munich, Munich, Germany
bSchool of Earth, Environment, and Sustainability, University of Iowa, Iowa City, IA, USA
cSenseable City Lab, Massachusetts Institute of Technology, Cambridge, MA, USA
Abstract
Geospatial algorithms have been developed through expert-driven discovery: a re-
searcher spots a limitation, proposes a structural fix, and checks it by hand. With
LLM-driven multi-agent systems becoming practical, much of the candidate-generation,
evaluation, and selection work can now be largely automated, while the researcher’s
role shifts upstream toward problem formulation, evaluation design, and interpretation.
We refer to this paradigm as Self-Evolving Geospatial Algorithms (SEGA) and propose
a framework with three required modules: a two-loop architecture with embedded geo-
graphic knowledge as the inner-loop engine; an automatic code formatter that converts
any raw geospatial algorithm into the standardized triple required by the inner loop;
and a simulation-driven training protocol, in which evolution runs only on synthetic
data with known ground truth, and the discovered algorithm is applied unchanged to
real data, keeping real-world results out-of-sample. We use spatial regime discovery as
a case study, seeded with the Two-stage K-Models algorithm. Evolution uses the Rand
Index against the ground-truth partition as fitness signal; the frozen algorithm is then
evaluated on 150 simulated grids and 11 real-world datasets across climate, health,
hydrology, and politics. The evolved algorithm outperforms its seed, knowledge-free
baselines, and four classical regionalization methods. Ablations further indicate that
the channel of geographic-knowledge injection, structured retrieval versus prompt-level
hints, is itself load-bearing. In this case study, LLM-assisted search sped up the inner
loop; whether it does so for other seeds and task families remains open. The geog-
rapher’s role — asking the right questions, designing trustworthy evaluation — grows
more central.
Keywords:
Geospatial modeling, large language models, algorithm discovery

1. Introduction
Geospatial modeling sits at the core of geospatial research, supporting tasks such
as spatial partitioning (Anselin and Amaral, 2024; Duque et al., 2007; Assunção et al.,
2006), prediction (Brunsdon et al., 1998; Fotheringham et al., 2002, 2017), spatial
dependence modeling (Anselin, 1988; LeSage and Pace, 2009; Anselin, 1995), and un-
certainty quantification (Lou et al., 2025). The development of these models has typ-
ically grown out of an expert-driven process that brings together theoretical insights,
empirical observations, and domain knowledge, often accumulating over decades of
methodological refinement (Cressie, 1993; Goodchild, 2004). Such development can be
characterized as expert-driven discovery: a researcher identifies a limitation, hypothe-
sizes a structural improvement (e.g., adding spatial weights, restructuring a clustering
objective, or proposing a new estimator), implements it, and validates it against es-
tablished baselines. Each discovery step is conceptually rich but is also human-paced,
costly in time, and naturally limited by the cognitive and institutional resources avail-
able to any single research group.
The rapid development of large language models (LLMs), including ChatGPT
(Singh et al., 2025), Gemini (Gemini Team et al., 2023), DeepSeek (Liu et al., 2024),
and Qwen (Yang et al., 2025), together with the rise of LLM-based multi-agent ar-
chitectures (Park et al., 2023), suggests that much of the routine engineering work of
algorithm development can now be largely automated. Working in this complementary
mode, the researcher delegates the work of generating candidate programs, evaluating
them, and keeping the better ones to an LLM-driven system, while retaining respon-
sibility for deciding what to optimize, setting up the evaluation, and making sense of
what comes out. Working in this mode, researchers spend less time writing and de-
bugging small algorithmic variants by hand, and more time on the upstream questions:
what is a good solution to this problem, what fitness signal captures it, and what do the
resulting algorithms tell us. The two modes are best seen as complementary: expert-
driven discovery continues to mark out the design space and the objectives that matter,
while LLM-assisted search systematically explores parts of that space that would be
tedious to cover manually (Novikov et al., 2025; Romera-Paredes et al., 2024). Within
geospatial science, the convergence of GeoAI (Janowicz et al., 2020; Mai et al., 2023)
and LLM-based agents is opening up new directions for spatial analysis and knowledge
discovery.
It is useful to distinguish at the outset between two complementary lines of LLM-
based research now active in geospatial science. The first treats the LLM as an or-
chestrator of a fixed library of pre-existing geospatial tools and algorithms: the model
interprets a user request, selects appropriate operations, and emits glue code that in-
vokes them, while the underlying spatial algorithms remain entirely human-authored.
We refer to this as the usage layer of the algorithm stack. The second treats the LLM
as an author that proposes and mutates algorithm source code itself, generating new
algorithmic logic rather than choosing among existing tools. We refer to this as the
design layer. The present paper, together with the GeoEvolve framework it builds on
(Luo et al., 2025), sits firmly at the design layer: the toolbox is the object that gets
evolved, not the menu that gets chosen from. Section 2 reviews both lines in detail and
identifies the specific inner-loop engines we adopt; here we only flag the distinction so
as to keep the technical premise of the rest of the paper visible.
2


--- Page 3 ---
The central message of the present paper is that the combination of these two
modes describes a noticeable shift in how geospatial algorithms can be developed,
and that this shift deserves to be named and characterized as such. We refer to this
LLM-assisted paradigm as Self-Evolving Geospatial Algorithms (SEGA), denoting a
structured, evaluation-driven search over the space of executable geospatial programs,
in which candidate algorithms are continuously generated, evaluated, and selected by
an LLM-powered multi-agent system. We propose a working hypothesis to guide its
scope: if the optimization objective of a geospatial problem can be specified clearly
enough for computational evaluation, the inner loop of algorithm development can be
largely delegated to a multi-agent LLM system, while the outer loop of formulating the
problem and interpreting the results remains the responsibility of the researcher. We
do not claim that algorithm design has become trivial; rather, we observe that, given
a well-defined objective, LLM-driven evolutionary systems can systematically explore
parts of the design space that are difficult to traverse manually.
A natural starting point for realizing SEGA is the recently proposed GeoEvolve
framework (Luo et al., 2025), which extends flat, single-loop, domain-agnostic evolu-
tionary engines such as OpenEvolve (Sharma, 2025) by wrapping the inner LLM-driven
code-evolution loop with an outer dialogue that retrieves geographic knowledge from
a curated corpus and injects it into the next mutation. This two-loop architecture
with embedded geographic knowledge is, in our view, the necessary substrate for any
practical SEGA system, and we adopt it as the inner-loop engine of our framework
without redesign. Two further extensions, however, are required before this engine
can be used routinely on new geospatial problems. The first concerns the input side:
raw geospatial algorithms are written in heterogeneous styles, and integrating each
new seed by hand re-introduces a manual-engineering bottleneck that the inner loop is
supposed to remove. An LLM-driven automatic code formatter that converts any raw
geospatial algorithm into the standardized triple (evolvable program, evaluator module,
configuration file) required by the inner loop is therefore needed to make the frame-
work reusable across tasks. The second concerns the evaluation side: when evolution
is driven directly by the algorithm’s performance on the very data on which its output
will be reported, real-world metrics become both training target and evaluation target,
and the resulting numbers tell us less than they appear to. A simulation-driven train-
ing protocol with a controlled data-generating process, in which evolution is run only on
synthetic data with a known ground truth and the discovered algorithm is then applied
unchanged to real data, is therefore needed to keep real-world results as out-of-sample
evidence rather than direct optimization targets. The three pieces together, GeoE-
volve’s two-loop architecture, an automatic code formatter, and a simulation-driven
training protocol, constitute the conceptual framework developed in the remainder of
this paper.
To make this paradigm shift concrete rather than abstract, the bulk of the paper
develops a case study on spatial regime discovery, taking the Two-stage K-Models
algorithm (Guo et al., 2023) as the seed algorithm A0.
We chose this case study
for three reasons: it represents the current state of the art among non-LLM spatial
regime methods, its two-stage structure of initial over-partitioning followed by region
merging exposes a small number of clearly evolvable modules that an LLM-driven inner
loop can target, and its piecewise-linear regime assumption admits a clean simulated
ground truth required by the train-on-simulation / apply-on-real evaluation protocol
3


--- Page 4 ---
described below. As a single case study, it shows that the framework works on this task;
applying it to further seeds and task families in future work is needed to establish that
it generalizes. A more complete account of the spatial regime literature and Two-stage
K-Models is given in Section 2.4.
Within the case study, evolution happens exclusively on simulated grids using a
single bounded fitness signal (Rand Index against the ground-truth partition); the re-
sulting algorithm is then applied unchanged to 11 real-world datasets across climate,
health, hydrology, and politics, where SSR, SSR Reduction, RMSE, and Variance Ratio
are used as evaluation metrics disjoint from the fitness signal. On top of this, we con-
duct a structured ablation that varies both the level and the specificity of geographic-
knowledge injection (details in Section 4.4.1), so as to test how (not merely whether)
domain knowledge should enter the inner loop of the two-loop architecture.
The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 reviews related work
on LLM-based autonomous agents, distinguishes earlier LLM-based search over short
programs and expressions (Section 2.2) from the more recent AlphaEvolve paradigm
of LLM-driven algorithm discovery (Section 2.3) on which this paper builds, and closes
with a background subsection on the spatial regime literature that motivates the case
study (Section 2.4). Section 3 develops the SEGA framework, with a conceptual sub-
section that frames the paradigm and formalizes it as a quintuple (Section 3.1) and a
detailed subsection that implements the three required modules (Section 3.2). Section 4
presents the spatial regime case study together with its experimental design, includ-
ing the problem definition, the simulation experiment with its six knowledge-injection
variants, and the real-world experiment with its four classical regionalization baselines.
Section 5 reports the empirical results on both simulated and real-world data. Section 6
discusses what the discovered algorithm modified, the insights and complementarity
with expert-driven design, and limitations, framed around the broader question of how
autonomous geospatial algorithm discovery should proceed. Section 7 concludes.
2. Related Works
2.1. LLM-based Autonomous Agents
LLM-based autonomous agents have begun to be explored in geographical infor-
mation science (GIScience), where agents are designed to support spatial analysis and
mapping workflows. Across this line of work the LLM operates at what we call the usage
layer of the algorithm stack: it acts as a decision core that interprets user intent and
orchestrates a fixed library of pre-existing geospatial tools, while the underlying spatial
algorithms remain entirely human-authored. Early studies use LLMs to translate spa-
tial problems into executable geoprocessing steps, ranging from spatial data retrieval
to invoking spatial algorithms (Zhang et al., 2023; Li and Ning, 2023). Multi-agent
pipelines have also been used to decompose spatial tasks into planner-worker struc-
tures for operations such as shapefile processing and spatial analysis (Lin et al., 2025).
Other work investigates automated geospatial data discovery agents that generate and
run programs to locate appropriate spatial datasets (Ning et al., 2025). By emulating
cartographic workflows, LLM agents can also be guided to design, add, or modify map
elements as part of an interactive mapping process (Zhang et al., 2024). Related ef-
forts include LLM-powered QGIS spatial-analysis copilots (Akinboyewa et al., 2025),
harness-engineered research agents that span the broader GIScience research lifecycle
4


--- Page 5 ---
(Zhou et al., 2026), and the wider autonomous-GIS research agenda (Li et al., 2025).
While these efforts demonstrate the value of LLM agents for assembling and orches-
trating existing spatial operations, they typically rely on pre-defined tools rather than
directly proposing new algorithmic structures. Recent work suggests that LLMs may
also support more open-ended forms of geospatial scientific exploration, in which agents
help propose hypotheses, identify candidate spatial patterns, and combine heteroge-
neous datasets to generate further insight.
2.2. LLM-Based Search over Short Programs and Expressions
The use of LLMs has prompted reconsideration of how new algorithms and math-
ematical expressions can be discovered. In contrast to the usage-layer agents reviewed
above, the systems considered here operate at the design layer of the algorithm stack:
the LLM is not selecting among existing algorithms but authoring them, generating
and mutating the source code that implements the algorithmic logic itself.
An early line of work treats the LLM as a high-level variation operator embed-
ded inside an evolutionary or search loop, applied to compact single-file programs.
Eureka (Ma et al., 2023) used an LLM to evolve dense reward functions for reinforce-
ment learning by editing short candidate programs.
LMX (Meyerson et al., 2024)
explored LLM-driven variation over linguistic genotypes as a generic operator. Fun-
Search (Romera-Paredes et al., 2024) applied the same idea to mathematical reasoning,
using the LLM to mutate short Python functions and reporting novel constructions for
problems such as the cap-set problem and online bin-packing. LLM-SR (Shojaee et al.,
2024) adapted symbolic regression in the same spirit, treating the discovery of compact
mathematical expressions as program search.
Common to these systems is that the unit being evolved is a single short function
or expression rather than the broader algorithmic framework in which it is embedded:
the LLM proposes local edits inside a few-line, single-file program. While these re-
sults demonstrate that LLM-driven search can produce novel solutions on well-scoped
function-level problems, the mutation envelope is too narrow to express the structural
moves required to evolve a full geospatial algorithm with multiple stages, parameters,
and data pipelines, for example swapping an initialization strategy, restructuring a clus-
tering objective, or adding a per-region penalty term. The next subsection introduces
the more recent line of work that targets this larger unit of evolution.
2.3. LLM-Driven Algorithm Discovery: The AlphaEvolve Paradigm
A second, more recent line of work targets the discovery of full algorithms rather
than short functions, by allowing the LLM to mutate program text spanning multiple
files and many lines of logic.
We refer to this as the AlphaEvolve paradigm.
The
three systems described below, AlphaEvolve as the original proposal, OpenEvolve as
its open-source implementation, and GeoEvolve as its first geospatial specialization,
jointly characterize this paradigm. Because this paper uses OpenEvolve and GeoEvolve
directly as the inner-loop engine Φ of Section 3 rather than proposing a new engine, this
subsection describes what each system actually provides before the case study begins.
AlphaEvolve. AlphaEvolve (Novikov et al., 2025) extends LLM-driven evolution from
single short functions to entire multi-file codebases, reporting measurable improvements
on long-standing algorithmic problems including matrix multiplication and other open
5


--- Page 6 ---
mathematical questions. The methodological move is significant: instead of evolving
a short single function of a few dozen lines, the system mutates and recomposes al-
gorithmic structures of hundreds of lines, including initialization strategies, iteration
schedules, and helper subroutines. This brings algorithm discovery, rather than merely
function discovery, within reach of LLM-driven search.
OpenEvolve. OpenEvolve (Sharma, 2025) is an open-source implementation in the
spirit of AlphaEvolve, packaging the same inner loop as a domain-agnostic engine.
Given a seed program with clearly marked evolvable blocks, a fitness function, and an
iteration budget, OpenEvolve executes a flat loop of propose mutation →run →eval-
uate →select. It is intentionally domain-agnostic: it carries no notion of geographic
space, no curated scientific corpus, and no mechanism for steering the search beyond
whatever text happens to be in the prompt. Within this paper, OpenEvolve serves
both as a standalone baseline, used directly with or without hand-written geographic-
knowledge hints in the prompt, and as the underlying mutation engine that GeoEvolve
wraps.
GeoEvolve. GeoEvolve (Luo et al., 2025) is the first geospatial specialization of the
AlphaEvolve paradigm: it wraps the OpenEvolve loop in three agent-level modules so
that geographic domain knowledge can enter each round of evolution through struc-
tured retrieval rather than only through static prompts. A Code Analyzer is a di-
agnostic LLM agent that reads the current evolved code together with its evaluation
metrics and outputs (in strict JSON) which pieces of geographic knowledge appear
missing or misapplied, along with search queries for the knowledge retriever and flags
indicating whether code examples or theoretical background are needed. A Knowledge
Retriever (GeoKnowRAG) maintains a curated corpus of geospatial documents and re-
turns ranked passages relevant to the Analyzer’s queries through retrieval-augmented
generation. The corpus, embedding model, vector store, and retrieval procedure are all
configurable; the specific choices used in this paper are documented in Appendix B. Fi-
nally, a Geo-informed Prompt Generator assembles the retrieved knowledge passages,
the analyzer’s diagnostic notes, and the current code into a structured prompt that is
fed back into the next OpenEvolve mutation step. The result is a two-loop architecture
in which geographic knowledge enters the search at the retrieval level, conditioned on
the current state of the evolved code, rather than only as fixed prompt context.
Implication for this paper. The distinction between OpenEvolve (prompt-level knowl-
edge only, if any) and GeoEvolve (prompt-level + retrieval-level geographic knowledge)
defines a natural design space for ablation. Section 4.4.1 uses this design space to
construct six algorithm variants spanning no knowledge, a general prompt hint, a task-
specific prompt hint, multi-agent dialogue without retrieval, and multi-agent dialogue
with full GeoKnowRAG, in addition to the unevolved seed. We use these six variants
across the case study to test the hypothesis that the channel of knowledge injection
(prompt versus retrieval) is itself a load-bearing design choice.
2.4. Spatial Regime Discovery
Because the case study (Section 4) is grounded in spatial regime discovery, we briefly
review the relevant methodological background here. Spatial regime modeling seeks to
partition a study area into contiguous subregions within which the data-generating
6


--- Page 7 ---
process relating covariates to a response variable is locally homogeneous but differs
across regions (Anselin, 1988; Anselin and Amaral, 2024).
It is a central method-
ological tool for handling spatial heterogeneity (Fotheringham et al., 2017) and sits
at the intersection of three long-standing traditions: contiguity-preserving regionaliza-
tion (Openshaw, 1977; Openshaw and Rao, 1995; Assunção et al., 2006; Duque et al.,
2007), geographically weighted regression (Brunsdon et al., 1998; Fotheringham et al.,
2002, 2017), and graph-based spatial clustering followed by regression (Helbich et al.,
2013). Recent work has unified these threads by embedding regression objectives di-
rectly into the partitioning procedure: Anselin and Amaral (2024) extend SKATER
with a regression-SSR cut criterion (Skater-reg), while Guo et al. (2023) propose Two-
stage K-Models, Regional-K-Models, and a regression-aware variant of the Automatic
Zoning Procedure. Among these, the Two-stage K-Models algorithm is reported by its
authors to “largely outperform existing approaches on model fitting, region reconstruc-
tion and coefficient estimation” (Guo et al., 2023), making it the strongest non-LLM
baseline currently available for spatial regime discovery. This is the algorithm we adopt
as the seed A0 throughout the case study; the rationale for this choice was previewed
in the Introduction.
3. Methods: The SEGA Framework
This section develops the SEGA framework introduced in Section 1. Section 3.1
sets up the concept and the division of labor between researcher and agent, formalized
as a quintuple. Section 3.2 then specifies each of the three required modules in turn.
3.1. Conceptualizing SEGA: From Paradigm Shift to Quintuple
The basic idea of SEGA is to treat algorithm development not as a replacement
for expert-driven design but as a complement to it: alongside the conceptual moves
researchers make by hand, parts of algorithm refinement can be carried out as a struc-
tured, evaluation-driven search over executable programs. Two observations motivate
this view. First, the historical record of geospatial algorithm development is domi-
nated by what we call expert-driven discovery: discrete, conceptually rich modifications
that come out of a researcher noticing a limitation and proposing a fix (for example,
adding spatial weights into a regression model, replacing a Euclidean dissimilarity with
a contiguity-aware one, or adding a penalty against spatially fragmented partitions).
These discoveries are valuable but slow, and the design space between them is large.
Second, LLMs and LLM-based multi-agent systems now provide the technical means
to automate large parts of the candidate-generation, evaluation, and selection process.
The resulting division of labor is straightforward: the agent system handles the genera-
tion, evaluation, and selection of variants on top of any given seed algorithm, while the
researcher retains responsibility for formulating the problem, designing the objective,
defining the evaluation, and interpreting the result. SEGA, in this sense, is an attempt
to make use of the second observation without giving up the first.
Figure 1 contrasts the two paradigms in stylized form. In the expert-driven paradigm
(right panel), progress relies on conceptual innovations from researchers; each contribu-
tion typically requires identifying a limitation, hypothesizing a structural modification,
implementing and testing it, and iterating. This process is inherently human-paced
and is naturally shaped by available time and disciplinary context. In the self-evolving
7


--- Page 8 ---
paradigm (left panel), candidate algorithms are continuously refined through auto-
mated mutation, evaluation, and selection within a unified computational framework,
but the researcher still owns the upstream decisions: what to optimize, what counts as
a good answer, and what the resulting algorithms tell us. Both modes have value: the
former provides conceptual depth, the latter offers breadth of exploration.
Figure 1: A schematic comparison of expert-driven discovery (green panel) and self-evolving discov-
ery (blue panel).
Expert-driven discovery typically advances through conceptual innovations con-
tributed by individual researchers and groups, whereas self-evolving discovery follows a more central-
ized, metric-driven evolutionary trajectory. In SEGA, the inner loop of how to refine an algorithm
is largely delegated to the agent, while the outer loop of what question to ask remains with the re-
searcher. The two paradigms are complementary rather than mutually exclusive.
Formalization as a quintuple. We formalize SEGA as a quintuple (A0, D, E, K, Φ). Here
A0 is the seed algorithm, an initial executable program implementing a baseline
geospatial method; D = {(si, Xi, Yi)}N
i=1 is the spatial dataset, with si ∈R2 the
spatial coordinates, Xi ∈RK the explanatory variables, and Yi the response variable;
E : A × D →Rm is the evaluation protocol, a mapping from an algorithm–dataset
pair to an m-dimensional performance vector that provides a fitness signal for evolu-
tionary selection; K is the geographic knowledge base, a curated corpus of spatial
theories, statistical methods, and established geographic principles; and Φ is the evolu-
tion engine, an LLM-powered operator that proposes structural variants of candidate
8


--- Page 9 ---
algorithms guided by performance feedback and domain knowledge. After T rounds
the system returns the discovered algorithm A⋆, its performance profile E(A⋆, D), and
(if logging is enabled) the evolution trace.
Humans define ‘what’, agents figure out ‘how’. The quintuple makes explicit which
components remain a researcher’s responsibility and which can be delegated to the
agent, and the division it draws is exactly the one shown in Figure 1: the researcher
defines the what, the question and the metric that counts as a good answer, while
the agent (in the self-evolving mode) figures out the how. Concretely, the researcher
chooses A0 (which existing algorithm to use as the starting point), constructs D (which
simulated and real-world data to use), designs E (what counts as a good solution
and how to measure it), and curates K (what geographic knowledge the system can
draw on); the agent, via Φ, handles the inner loop, generating candidate variants of
A0, running them on D, scoring them with E, and selecting which to keep. Three
modules are required to turn this abstract quintuple into a system that can actually
be applied to a new geospatial problem, and they are exactly the three pieces flagged
in the Introduction: the Evolution Engine
1
(Section 3.2.1), the Code Formatter
2 (Section 3.2.2), and the Simulation-Driven Training Protocol
3 (Section 3.2.3).
Figure 2 provides the abstract block-level architecture of SEGA; Figure 3 expands each
of the three modules to show, in an infographic form, the agent-level workings inside
them.

3.2. Implementing SEGA: Three Required Modules
3.2.1. Module
1 : Two-Loop Architecture with Embedded Geographic Knowledge
The first module specifies how the evolution engine Φ is organized so that geographic
domain knowledge K can be brought to bear on each round of mutation. We require a
two-loop architecture: an inner loop that performs LLM-driven code evolution (propose
mutation →run →evaluate →select), wrapped by an outer loop that analyzes the
current evolved code, retrieves relevant geographic knowledge from K, and feeds the
retrieved knowledge back into the next inner-loop mutation as a structured prompt.
The inner loop is responsible for exploring the space of algorithmic variants; the outer
loop is responsible for steering that exploration with established geographic theory.
Formally, the inner loop computes
A⋆= arg
min
A∈ΦT (P0) L(A, Dsim),
(1)
where P0 is the initial candidate set seeded from A0, ΦT(·) is the evolutionary process
over T iterations, L is the fitness function, and Dsim is the simulated dataset used
during evolution (the use of Dsim rather than D is enforced by Module
3 below).
Adopted realization: GeoEvolve. The two-loop architecture is the central methodolog-
ical innovation of GeoEvolve (Luo et al., 2025), distinguishing it from flat, single-
loop, domain-agnostic engines such as OpenEvolve (Sharma, 2025) in which geographic
11


--- Page 12 ---
knowledge can enter only as static prompt text. We adopt GeoEvolve as our off-the-
shelf inner-loop engine, with its default agent architecture, prompts, and hyperparam-
eters from the original paper (background on the four agents is given in Section 2.3);
the top dashed panel ( 1 ) of Figure 2 shows how the four agents are wired together
within the Evolution Engine Φ. In practice we use the open-source Python package
geoevolve released alongside Luo et al. (2025), which packages the entire two-loop
architecture (Code Evolver, Code Analyzer, Knowledge Retriever, and Geo-informed
Prompt Generator) behind a single configuration interface, so that adopting GeoEvolve
as the inner-loop engine requires no re-implementation.
Design space of knowledge integration. A practical question remains open even after
adopting GeoEvolve: how geographic knowledge enters Φ through the outer loop. We
characterize the design space along two axes. The first axis is the level at which knowl-
edge is injected: prompt-level injection encodes domain knowledge as natural-language
instructions in a static prompt, whereas retrieval-level injection dynamically retrieves
relevant knowledge from a curated corpus and conditions it on the current state of
the evolved code. The second axis is the specificity of the injected knowledge: none,
general (e.g., Tobler’s first law, spatial autocorrelation, scale effects), or task-specific
(e.g., contiguity penalties, region-size balancing for spatial regimes). The combination
of these two axes defines the six algorithm variants used in our case-study ablation
(Section 4.4.1).
3.2.2. Module
2 : Automatic Code Formatter
The second module operates on the seed algorithm A0: it specifies how a raw
geospatial algorithm, written in whatever style its authors prefer, is turned into the
standardized input that the inner-loop engine Φ requires.
Without this step every
new seed requires manual engineering before evolution can begin; with it, the same
evolutionary infrastructure is designed to be reusable across different seeds and tasks
with little or no manual adaptation. We state this as a property of the design rather
than a demonstrated one: the formatter is exercised here on a single seed (Section 4),
and whether it generalizes across algorithm families remains untested (Section 6.5).
We define the formatting problem as a transformation that takes a raw geospatial
algorithm Araw as input and returns a standardized triple
Format(Araw) →(Ainit, Eeval, Cconfig),
(2)
in which Ainit is an initial program with clearly marked evolvable blocks and a stan-
dardized entry function that returns predictions together with any auxiliary outputs
(region labels, coefficients, etc.) needed by the evaluation step; Eeval is an evaluator
module that implements the evaluation protocol E and computes the fitness signal and
the held-out evaluation metrics from the algorithm’s outputs; and Cconfig is a configu-
ration specification that records the evolutionary hyperparameters (population size,
number of iterations, mutation strategy) and any task-specific settings (target number
of regions, convergence criteria, soft constraints). This standardized triple acts as a
contract between the candidate algorithm and the inner-loop engine: regardless of how
the underlying algorithm is written, each candidate exposes a uniform interface for
execution, evaluation, and comparison.
12


--- Page 13 ---
In our implementation, the formatting step itself is performed automatically by
an LLM-driven parser: given a raw script that solves a geospatial task in some style,
the parser identifies the core algorithmic logic, marks the evolvable blocks, generates
the standardized entry function, writes the evaluator module against the user-specified
metrics, and emits a configuration file together with metadata for traceability. Re-
searchers therefore only need to provide a working implementation of their geospatial
algorithm; the engineering work of preparing it for evolutionary search is handled by
the formatter. We use this formatter to prepare the Two-stage K-Models seed used
throughout the case study. A worked example of the formatter operating on the Two-
stage K-Models seed is provided in Appendix E, showing the raw input, the resulting
evolvable program Ainit with marked blocks, the generated evaluator module Eeval, and
the configuration Cconfig.
3.2.3. Module
3 : Simulation-Driven Training Protocol with a Controlled DGP
The third module operates on the pair (D, E): it specifies what dataset the inner
loop is allowed to see during evolution, and what metric the inner loop is asked to opti-
mize. We argue that these two choices should be made together, and at the framework
level, because they determine whether the resulting algorithm is being evolved against
something geographically meaningful or simply against statistical convenience. Con-
cretely, we propose three principles, all centered on the idea of training on a controlled
simulator and evaluating on real data.
Principle 1: Run the inner loop only on synthetic data. The inner loop Φ is run only
on a synthetic dataset Dsim whose ground-truth structure S⋆is known by construction
(for example, a known partition, a known surface, or a known set of intervals). S⋆
gives a clear, unambiguous fitness signal, and the real-world data is never seen by the
mutation, selection, or knowledge-retrieval steps, so real-world results count as out-
of-sample evidence rather than as a target the system has quietly been optimizing
against.
Principle 2: Apply the discovered algorithm directly, without further tuning on real data.
After T rounds, the discovered algorithm A⋆is frozen and applied unchanged to each
real-world dataset. No hyperparameters are retuned, no additional evolution rounds
are run, and no knowledge retrieval is done on the real-world side. Any performance
difference observed on real-world data can then be attributed to the structure of A⋆
itself, rather than to per-dataset adjustments.
Principle 3: Use different metrics for driving the search and for reporting results. The
metrics in the system play two distinct roles. A fitness signal drives the inner loop Φ;
its purpose is to steer the search toward better algorithms. Evaluation metrics describe
the discovered algorithm after the search is over; their purpose is to tell the reader how
well it actually performs. We recommend keeping these two sets separate, because
using the same metric in both roles is uninformative: any algorithm produced by an
evolutionary search that explicitly optimizes a metric M will, by construction, score
well on M.
What makes a good fitness signal?. Within these three principles, a useful fitness signal
is a bounded, dimensionless metric that compares the algorithm’s output to the ground-
truth structure S⋆directly. Examples include clustering-agreement indices such as the
13


--- Page 14 ---
Rand Index for partitioning tasks, coverage–width scores for prediction-interval tasks,
and bounded ranking measures for retrieval tasks. Such fitness signals are bounded
(the search has a stable target), robust to trivial structural choices (they cannot be
gamed by simply producing more, smaller regions, as SSR-family metrics can), and
on a different scale from the usual evaluation metrics, which keeps the evaluation set
genuinely held-out.
One intended consequence of these principles is that the same protocol should be
reusable, with minor adjustments, across very different SEGA tasks: only Dsim, S⋆,
the fitness signal, and the evaluation metrics need to be re-specified per task, while the
surrounding inner-loop machinery is held fixed. This too is a consequence of the design
rather than a result: the protocol is instantiated here for one task (Section 4.2.1), and
whether the re-specification is as contained as the argument suggests is a question for
the further demonstrations called for in Section 6.5.
4. Case Study: Spatial Regime Algorithm Discovery
In this section we apply SEGA to spatial regime discovery. Section 4.1 states the
problem and the seed algorithm. Section 4.2 describes the simulation experiment used
to evolve the algorithm, including the simulator and the fitness signal. Section 4.3
describes the real-world experiment used as held-out evaluation, including the eleven
datasets across four domains. Section 4.4 then specifies the ten algorithms compared
throughout both experiments: six Two-stage K-Models variants (the unevolved seed
and five evolved variants spanning a 2×3 knowledge-injection design) and four classical
regionalization baselines. The same ten algorithms are evaluated under the same pro-
tocol in both the simulation experiment (Section 5.2) and the real-world experiment
(Section 5.3).
4.1. Problem Definition and Seed Algorithm
Spatial regime modeling. Let S ∈R2 be a geographical area partitioned into R mutually
exclusive and exhaustive subregions:
S =
R
[
r=1
Sr, Sr ∩Sr′ = ∅for r̸ = r′.
(3)
For an observational unit i located at si ∈S, a spatial regime exists when the data
generation process differs across these spatial partitions:
Yi = Fr(i)(Xi) + ϵi,
(4)
where Fr : RK →R is a regime-specific functional relationship, ϵi is an error term,
Yi is the dependent variable, and Xi = {xi,1, ..., xi,K} is the vector of K independent
variables for spatial unit i. The objective of spatial regime modeling is to reduce within-
region structural variability while increasing between-region structural differentiation
in the data generation mechanism. Spatial regime discovery is thus a descriptive par-
titioning task, in the same family as clustering and regionalization: given the observed
units of a study area, the algorithm assigns each unit to a regime and fits regime-
specific relationships, and the recovered regime structure is itself the analytical result
— a characterization of how the data-generating process varies across the study area.
14


--- Page 15 ---
Unlike predictive spatial models, a regime model makes no prediction at unobserved
locations and assigns no regime to units outside the data it partitions; its outputs
are evaluated by how well the partition accounts for structural heterogeneity within
the given data, in the same way that a fitted regression is summarized by its good-
ness of fit. This distinction determines how the algorithms in this paper are evaluated
(Section 4.3.1).
Seed algorithm: Two-stage K-Models. We use the Two-stage K-Models (2KModels) al-
gorithm (Guo et al., 2023) as the seed algorithm A0. 2KModels is a two-stage method
that first partitions a region into M subregions {S1, ..., SM} (with M > R a hyperpa-
rameter controlling the number of initial clusters), and then iteratively merges these
subregions into geographically connected regions until R regions are reached. As dis-
cussed in Section 2.4, 2KModels is the current state of the art among non-LLM spatial
regime methods.
4.2. Simulation Experiment
4.2.1. Design
We instantiate the train-on-simulation / apply-on-real protocol of Section 3.2.3 for
spatial regime discovery as follows.
Simulated datasets. We generated a series of datasets to evaluate the performance of
both the original and evolved versions of the spatial regime algorithm under known
ground-truth spatial regimes. Given the response variable Y and explanatory variables
X1, X2, the data generation process (DGP) is defined as:
Y = β0(u, v) + β1(u, v)X1 + β2(u, v)X2 + ϵ,
(5)
where X1, X2 ∼U[0, 1), i.i.d,
(6)
ϵ ∼N(0, σ2), i.i.d.
(7)
where (u, v) is one of 625 georeferenced observations on a 25 × 25 regular grid, U[0, 1) is
the uniform distribution on [0, 1), N(0, σ2) is the normal distribution with mean 0 and
variance σ2, and βi(u, v) are spatially varying coefficients that change across regions.
The grid is divided into five spatially connected regions S⋆= {S⋆
1, ..., S⋆
5} that consti-
tute the ground-truth partition. The intercept term β0 is set to 0, and the covariate
coefficients β1, β2 take values in {−2, −1, 0, 1, 2} depending on the subregion of each
cell. Three latent spatial regime patterns are used. In the Rectangular pattern, the
grid is split into five rectangular regions, each sized 5 × 25 units. In the Voronoi pat-
tern, five cells are randomly chosen as seeds and the resulting Voronoi diagram defines
five spatially contiguous regions. In the Arbitrary pattern, five cells are randomly
chosen as seeds and each seed expands at random to generate five connected regions.
We produce 150 grids in total at the high-noise level, evenly split across the three
patterns.
Fitness signal: Rand Index. Following Principle 3 of Module
3 (Section 3.2.3), the
inner loop Φ optimizes a single bounded fitness signal that compares the algorithm’s
output against the ground-truth partition S⋆. We use the Rand Index (RandI):
RandI =
TP + TN
TP + FN + FP + TN
(8)
15


--- Page 16 ---
where TP, FN, FP, and TN denote true positive, false negative, false positive, and
true negative pairs of cells, respectively. RandI is bounded in [0, 1], robust to inflated
k (it penalizes both over- and under-segmentation), and disjoint in scale from the
SSR-family metrics reserved for post-hoc evaluation. It is the only metric the inner
loop Φ sees: the LLM-driven mutation, selection, and knowledge-retrieval steps do not
access SSR, RMSE, or any other downstream metric. For computational tractability,
the inner loop does not evaluate every candidate program on all 150 grids; instead,
evolution operates on a fixed subset of three representative grids, one per spatial pattern
(Rectangular #5, Voronoi #75, Arbitrary #149), and the per-round fitness reported
during evolution is the mean RandI across these three grids. The discovered algorithm
A⋆is then evaluated, frozen, on the full 150-grid pool in Section 5.2; the per-round
fitness during evolution (mean RandI over the three training grids) and the per-pattern
metrics in Table 3 (means over the full 150-grid pool, which contains those three
grids) are therefore aggregated over different grid sets and are not directly comparable;
excluding the three training grids from the 150-grid evaluation changes the reported
means by less than 0.2 SSR and 0.001 ARI.
Evaluation-harness isolation. The harness prevents a generated candidate from ever
seeing the ground-truth partition.
A candidate receives only (X, Y, w, p, min_size)
through a fixed entry point and returns a label vector; RandI is computed by the har-
ness outside the candidate’s process, and a static scan rejects, with fitness zero, any
program that references ground-truth labels, computes label-agreement metrics inter-
nally, or performs file or network I/O. Every program generated in the reported runs
was additionally audited for ground-truth references; none were found. The discovered
algorithm’s own internal objective is likewise label-free — it selects among candidate
partitions by post-merge SSR under a connectivity constraint — so the frozen algorithm
runs on real data, where no ground truth exists, exactly as it does on simulation.
Inner-loop budget and LLM backbone. Each of the five evolved variants runs for the
same total budget of 100 inner-loop iterations. The framework is LLM-agnostic in
principle; in this case study we use a weighted pair of OpenAI models accessed through
OpenRouter: openai/gpt-4o as the primary model (sampling weight 0.8) and openai/gpt-4.1
as the secondary model (weight 0.2), with sampling parameters temperature = 0.7,
top_p = 0.95, and max_tokens = 8192. The same backbone is shared by all four GeoE-
volve agents. Full hyperparameter settings, including the MAP-Elites population and
GeoKnowRAG configuration, are reported in Appendix B.
4.3. Real-world Experiment
4.3.1. Design
Following Principle 2 of Module
3 (Section 3.2.3), the algorithm discovered on
simulation is frozen and applied unchanged to each real-world dataset, with no further
evolution, no hyperparameter retuning, and no knowledge retrieval on the real-world
side. All algorithms in the real-world comparison are run with the same target number
of regions p (inferred from administrative units) and the same six-nearest-neighbor
spatial weights matrix. Because each variant was evolved three times (Section 5.2), one
program per variant must be carried forward to the real-world study. We select, for
each variant, the run with the best simulation performance, and freeze that program;
the selection uses simulation results only and no real-world data, so the real-world
16


--- Page 17 ---
evaluation remains out-of-sample with respect to both evolution and selection. This
is the best-of-N protocol a practitioner would follow — run the search a few times,
keep the best algorithm — and we report it explicitly because it means the real-world
numbers reflect the best attainable program per variant rather than the average one.
The corresponding distributions across all three runs are the ones given in Table 3.
Evaluation metrics. Following Principle 3 of Module
3 , the metrics used to report
real-world performance are disjoint from the RandI fitness signal that drives the in-
ner loop. Because regime discovery is a descriptive partitioning task (Section 4.1),
the quantities below are model-fit statistics — how much structural heterogeneity a
partition accounts for — computed by the evaluation harness identically for every al-
gorithm, with the same target number of regions p, the same spatial weights, and the
same data. Whether an algorithm recovers the correct regime structure is established
on the simulated data, where ground truth exists and agreement is measured by ARI
(Section 5.2); the real-world study then asks whether the algorithm discovered there
— the best simulation run per variant, frozen with no further evolution or tuning —
transfers unchanged to data it has never seen. Let {(Xi, Yi)} denote the dataset and
ˆYi = F(Xi) the predictions of a candidate algorithm. We use four evaluation metrics.
The Sum of Squared Residuals (SSR) measures absolute prediction error,
SSR =

where Fr is the regime-specific fit on region Sr. The SSR Reduction ratio summarizes
the proportional improvement of a multi-regime spatial model over a single global OLS
fit:
SSR Reduction = 1 −

The Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) reports cross-dataset prediction accuracy
as the root mean squared deviation between predicted and observed Y . These four
metrics are computed post-hoc and are never fed back into the evolution loop, so the
LLM cannot game them.

4.4. Comparison Methods
Both the simulation experiment (Section 4.2) and the real-world experiment (Sec-
tion 4.3) compare the same ten algorithms under a unified protocol. The ten algorithms
fall into two groups: six Two-stage K-Models variants, which share an algorithmic an-
cestry with the seed and isolate the effect of LLM-driven evolution along a structured
knowledge-injection design; and four classical regionalization baselines, drawn from
the broader spatial regime / regionalization literature, which examine whether any
observed gains generalize beyond the K-Models family.
4.4.1. Six Two-stage K-Models variants
The six variants in this group share the Two-stage K-Models seed as their com-
mon starting point. The unevolved seed acts as the no-evolution lower bound. The
remaining five variants span a 2×3 design that crosses the level at which geographic
knowledge enters the search (prompt-level vs. retrieval-level) with the specificity of
that knowledge (none / general / task-specific). Table 2 summarizes the design; the
corresponding runtime configuration is given in Appendix B.

Table 2: Six Two-stage K-Models variants placed along the two-axis knowledge-injection design.
“Multi-agent dialogue” indicates whether the Code Analyzer / Knowledge Retriever / Prompt Gen-
erator loop is active. “Analyzer-generated” indicates that the prompt content is produced at runtime
by the Code Analyzer rather than written by hand. All five evolved variants run for the same total
budget of 100 inner-loop iterations.
This design allows us to decompose what would otherwise be a single “GeoEvolve
vs. seed” comparison into two more informative sub-questions. The first asks whether
multi-agent control is needed, or whether a static knowledgeable prompt already suf-
fices. Comparing OpenEvolve (Specific GeoKnow.), which encodes task-specific geo-
graphic hints in a fixed prompt, against GeoEvolve (No GeoKnowRAG), which has the
same agent dialogue but no curated knowledge corpus, isolates the contribution of the
outer analyzer / prompt-generator loop. The second asks whether retrieval-level knowl-
edge dominates prompt-level knowledge. Comparing all three OpenEvolve variants (no,
18


--- Page 19 ---
general, or task-specific prompt) against the full GeoEvolve pipeline isolates the con-
tribution of structured retrieval through GeoKnowRAG over static prompt-encoded
hints. We hold the total evolutionary budget constant at 100 inner-loop iterations
across all five evolved variants, so any performance difference reflects the structure of
the inner loop rather than search-budget disparities.
4.4.2. Four classical regionalization baselines
A natural concern is that all six K-Models variants share the same algorithmic an-
cestry: the evolved variants are obtained by applying LLM-driven evolutionary search
to the Two-stage K-Models seed. To examine whether the observed gains generalize
beyond this seed family, we additionally compare against four representative algorithms
drawn from the broader spatial regime / regionalization literature. The four baselines
span distinct algorithmic paradigms developed over the past decades.
AZP is the regression-aware variant (Guo et al., 2023) of the classical Auto-
matic Zoning Procedure (Openshaw, 1977; Openshaw and Rao, 1995) that performs
local moves of border units between regions while preserving spatial contiguity and
minimum-size constraints, accepting moves that reduce the total within-region SSR.
Region-K-Models (Guo et al., 2023) is a partitioning method that iteratively reas-
signs each unit to the region whose local OLS fit best explains its observation, subject
to spatial-neighbor and connectivity constraints. GWR-Skater (Helbich et al., 2013)
is a two-stage approach that first estimates location-specific regression coefficients via
Geographically Weighted Regression and then clusters the resulting coefficient surface
using SKATER, a minimum-spanning-tree-based regionalization algorithm. Skater-
reg (Anselin and Amaral, 2024) is an extension of SKATER that uses regression-fit
residuals as the dissimilarity measure when cutting edges of the minimum spanning
tree, directly aligning the partitioning objective with regression-fit quality.
The four classical baselines are matched to the K-Models variants on protocol (same
target number of regions p, same six-nearest-neighbor spatial weights, same evaluation
metrics) but differ in algorithmic family, so any performance gap reflects modeling-
philosophy differences rather than implementation disparities.
5. Empirical Results: Simulated and Real-world Studies
This section reports the empirical results of running the ten algorithms (six Two-
stage K-Models variants from Section 4.4.1, and four classical regionalization baselines
from Section 4.4.2) under the unified evaluation protocol of Section 4. We begin in
Section 5.1 by introducing the algorithm discovered by SEGA as a new spatial regime
model in its own right, comparing it with the Two-stage K-Models seed and tracing
how the inner loop arrived at it over ten evolutionary rounds. Section 5.2 then reports
simulation performance on the full 150-grid evaluation set, and Section 5.3 reports
the real-world results, focusing on GeoEvolve versus the four classical baselines; the
detailed cross-variant comparison within the K-Models family on real-world data is
provided in Appendix F.
5.1. The Evolved Algorithm: GeoEvolve-2KModels
We refer to the algorithm produced by SEGA on the Two-stage K-Models seed as
GeoEvolve-2KModels. This subsection introduces it as a new spatial regime model in
19


--- Page 20 ---
its own right: how it differs structurally from the original 2KModels, how the inner
loop arrived at those differences over ten evolutionary rounds, and what geographic-
knowledge themes are embodied in the result.
Structural differences from the 2KModels seed. Compared with the original 2KModels,
the discovered algorithm introduces two structural refinements, both visible in the
round-by-round trace of Figure 4. First, the number of first-stage clusters is no
longer a fixed hyperparameter: where the seed always over-partitions into 20 clusters,
the discovered algorithm evaluates a small candidate set (2.5p, 4p, √n, and p to p+2),
runs each candidate through the merge stage, and keeps the partition with the lowest
post-merge SSR — turning a hand-set constant into an internal model-selection step.
Second, it appends a connectivity-preserving batch border-refinement stage:
after merging, border units are reassigned between adjacent regimes whenever the move
lowers a spatially penalized SSR, subject to two connectivity checks that guarantee
both the donor and the acceptor region remain contiguous, with early stopping under
a patience rule bounding the added cost. Both refinements select internally by label-
free SSR; neither involves any agreement-with-ground-truth quantity (Section 4.2.1).

Figure 4: Round-by-round trajectory of the SEGA inner-loop search starting from the Two-stage
K-Models seed, for the GeoEvolve (GeoKnowRAG) run reported in this paper. Annotated rounds
add new ideas (+, green), code modifications (⟲, orange), or parameter changes ({#}, blue), with
per-round scores marked in the figure. The plotted score is the inner-loop fitness: the mean Rand
Index across the three grids used during evolution (Rectangular #5, Voronoi #75, Arbitrary #149;
Section 4.2.1), rising from 0.9482 at the seed to 0.9852 at round 10. The vertical axis is truncated
because RandI is inflated by chance agreement on this task; the round-by-round changes, and the
chance-corrected held-out results, are described in the text.
How the evolution unfolded over ten rounds. Figure 4 traces the inner-loop trajectory
of the GeoEvolve (GeoKnowRAG) run across ten rounds, during which the mean Rand
Index on the three training grids rises from 0.9482 at the seed to 0.9852. The gain is
concentrated in the first three rounds, which contribute +0.0334 of the total +0.0370;
20


--- Page 21 ---
the remaining seven rounds add +0.0036 between them, and three of those rounds (5,
6 and 8) accept no new variant at all. Round 1 adds a border-unit reassignment
step guarded by two connectivity checks, so that a unit only moves to a neighbouring
region when both the donor and the acceptor remain spatially connected, and raises
the number of restarts from 4 to 10; this operationalizes the geographic principle that
adjacent units are more likely to share a regime than distant ones (Tobler’s first law
(Tobler, 1970)) as a local, topology-preserving move rather than a global re-partition.
Round 2 converts that step from per-unit to batch reassignment, evaluating all can-
didate moves and applying the best-gain set in one pass, and lifts the score to 0.9645
— the single largest jump before round 3. Round 3 makes the one change that al-
ters the algorithm’s search space: the number of first-stage clusters, fixed at 20 in
the seed, becomes a small search over 2.5p, 4p and √n, each run through the merge
stage and selected by SSR; the same round adds a spatial penalty on border moves
and early stopping with patience, and the score reaches 0.9816. Rounds 4–10 tune this
machinery rather than extend it: the candidate set is widened to include p, p + 1 and
p+2, the spatial penalty is annealed from 0.35 to 0.29 with a small deterministic jitter
for diversity across restarts, and the refinement budget is adjusted between 30 and
36 iterations with patience 3–4, ending at 0.9852. The end-of-trajectory algorithm is
the GeoEvolve-2KModels reported in the remainder of this paper. Two cautions apply
to this figure. First, the trajectory score is the mean RandI over the three training
grids #5, #75 and #149 and is therefore not comparable with the per-pattern val-
ues in Table 3, which are computed on the 150-grid pool; the same algorithm scores
0.9634 RandI there. Second, RandI is the optimization signal rather than an indepen-
dent measure of quality, and it is inflated by chance agreement on this task, which is
why Table 3 reports the chance-corrected ARI as the agreement metric. A complete
round-by-round trace of this evolutionary process, including the full source code at
each round, the LLM-generated edits, and the per-round fitness, is provided as an in-
teractive web page, linked from the project page (https://peng-luo.com/sega/), as
a supplement to Figure 4.
Geographic-knowledge themes embodied in the evolved algorithm. Across these refine-
ments, three geographic-knowledge themes are repeatedly invoked. On spatial con-
tiguity, every border-unit move is guarded by two connectivity checks that guarantee
both the donor and the acceptor region remain spatially connected — the algorithm
treats contiguity as a hard constraint to be preserved through every local improve-
ment, not repaired afterwards. On local spatial dependence, the border-refinement
stage operationalizes Tobler’s first law (Tobler, 1970): reassignments are confined to
units on regime boundaries, where a unit’s regime membership is most uncertain and
most informed by its neighbours, and a spatial penalty on border moves discourages
jagged, noise-driven boundaries. On scale as a modelling choice, the search over
the number of first-stage clusters (2.5p, 4p, √n) treats the initial partition scale not as
a fixed hyperparameter but as a quantity to be selected against the data by post-merge
SSR, echoing the sensitivity of regionalization outcomes to the chosen unit scale. The
broader interpretation of these themes for autonomous geospatial algorithm discovery
is taken up in Section 6.1.
21


--- Page 22 ---
5.2. Simulation Results
Performance on the simulated grids. The K-Models family outperforms the four clas-
sical regionalization baselines by a wide margin under the same protocol (Table 3): the
baselines’ average SSR ranges from ≈206 (AZP) to ≈403 (Skater-reg) against ≈68–87
for the family, and their ARI from 0.330 to 0.624 against 0.806–0.869 — a separa-
tion an order of magnitude larger than any run-to-run spread, and consistent with the
fact that the simulated data follow a piecewise-linear regime model whose assumption
2KModels and its descendants share but methods clustering GWR coefficient surfaces
or attribute distances do not directly optimize. Within the evolved family, averaged
over three independent runs, GeoEvolve with GeoKnowRAG attains the best three-
pattern averages — SSR 67.53 ± 18.24, ARI 0.869 ± 0.027, a 14.9% SSR reduction and
a +0.057 ARI gain over the seed — but it does not dominate every pattern (GeoEvolve
without GeoKnowRAG has the lower SSR on Voronoi and Arbitrary), and the effect of
geographic knowledge is non-monotone: OpenEvolve without geographic knowledge is
worse than the seed it started from (SSR 86.64 versus 79.38; ARI 0.806 versus 0.812),
a general knowledge prompt improves SSR to 72.95, a task-specific one only to 78.30.
Because the run-to-run standard deviations (5.32–18.24 on average SSR) are of the
same order as the gaps between variants (67.53–86.64), we report the ordering among
evolved variants as descriptive rather than as evidence that one is reliably better than
another. Complementing this run-to-run view, the discovered algorithm itself is reli-
ably better than the seed on the evaluation pool: a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test
over the 150 grids gives a median SSR improvement of 15.0 (p < 10−23) and a median
ARI gain of 0.080 (p < 10−17). Finally, the runtime column shows that the cost of
the accuracy gain is not intrinsic: the evolved algorithms range from 0.91 to 10.45
seconds per grid, excluding one run without early stopping that averages 188.9 s, an
ordering that follows how much search each performs at inference time rather than
how accurate it is; full token, elapsed-time and inference-time accounting is given in
Appendix C. A matched-budget control confirms that these gains are not an artifact
of additional search effort. Giving the unmodified seed the same cluster-count search
with random restarts, under the evolved algorithm’s own per-grid time budget, does
narrow the SSR gap — SSR being the quantity any such search optimizes directly —
but still leaves it short on recovery of the true regime structure, which is what the task
is defined on and which the comparison should therefore be read on (ARI 0.854 versus
0.894, p = 2.3 × 10−10); one-component ablations locate the advantage in the border-
refinement stage and its spatial penalty rather than in the cluster-count search — the
penalty being a component whose value is negative in the algorithm’s own selection
objective, which no tuning of the seed’s parameters against that objective could have
reached (Appendix D).
Figure 5 illustrates the reconstructed spatial regimes on the three grids used during
SEGA evolution (Rectangular #5, Voronoi #75, Arbitrary #149), comparing the seed,
the two best evolved variants, and the four classical regionalization baselines on the
same grids. Within the K-Models family, both evolved versions of 2KModels produce
regions that resemble the ground truth, while the original 2KModels exhibits some
misidentified boundaries and less coherent regions; the GeoEvolve-evolved version is
the closest to the ground truth across all three patterns. The four classical baselines re-
veal a sharper qualitative gap: AZP and Region-K-Models produce visibly fragmented
partitions, particularly on the Rectangular grid where the ground-truth structure is the

loses coherence on Voronoi and Arbitrary; Skater-reg merges the central regions and re-
duces the partition to two or three dominant regions on all three patterns. These visual
differences are consistent with the SSR gap reported in Table 3, which the K-Models
family closes by directly optimizing within-region regression fit.

5.3. Real-world Results
We now turn from simulated data, where the ground-truth partition is known and
the fitness signal can be evaluated directly, to real-world data, where neither is avail-
able and the discovered algorithm is asked to generalize out of sample.
We apply
23


--- Page 24 ---
the frozen GeoEvolve algorithm to the 11 real-world datasets and compare it against
the unevolved Two-stage K-Models seed and the four classical regionalization base-
lines under the unified evaluation protocol of Section 4.3.1. Figure 6 reports a com-
pact ten-algorithm SSR-Reduction summary by domain (which also includes the three
OpenEvolve variants and GeoEvolve without GeoKnowRAG), and Table 4 reports
cross-dataset means on the four quality metrics for the six-algorithm main comparison
(seed, four classical baselines, GeoEvolve). The detailed within-family comparison of
all six K-Models variants on real-world data (per-dataset, four-metric breakdown, with
corresponding regime maps and dominant-covariate maps) is provided in Appendix F.
Compared with the simulation, the real-world picture is more nuanced.
GeoEvolve attains the lowest cross-dataset average RMSE (1.220) and the highest
SSR Reduction (0.658), with nine first-place wins on SSR Reduction out of 11 datasets,
six wins on average R2, and five wins on RMSE, more than any other algorithm on
all three metrics; on Variance Ratio it has the highest mean (0.482) and four wins
(second to Skater-reg’s five). AZP reaches the highest mean R2 (0.830) and is the
most competitive classical baseline on per-dataset R2 and RMSE wins (4 each out of
11), illustrating that older regionalization methods remain competitive on individual
datasets when the underlying regimes are nearly piecewise constant in the response
variable. The unevolved 2KModels seed (mean R2 0.816, mean SSR Reduction 0.625)
holds its own as a strong baseline, ahead of all four classical baselines on SSR Reduction.
Among the four classical regionalization baselines, three (Region-K-Models, GWR-
Skater, Skater-reg) fall noticeably behind on SSR Reduction (0.488–0.582 vs. 0.658 for
GeoEvolve and 0.625 for the seed).
Two qualitative conclusions follow. First, an algorithm discovered entirely on simu-
lated grids transfers to real data without modification: GeoEvolve is competitive with,
or better than, every classical regionalization baseline on real-world data, despite the
simulator being matched to the K-Models modeling assumption. The claim here is
about transfer of the algorithm, not about predictive generalization to unobserved lo-
cations: these are fit statistics on the datasets being partitioned (Section 4.3.1), and
what they show is that a procedure developed against a synthetic regime model re-
mains well behaved on empirical data whose generating process it was never shown.
Second, no single algorithm dominates across all metrics and all datasets: AZP is
unexpectedly strong on R2, Skater-reg wins the most datasets on Variance Ratio de-
spite a lower mean, and GeoEvolve provides the tightest regression fit, the largest SSR
Reduction, and the highest mean Variance Ratio. This suggests that performance is
metric-dependent and that practitioners should consider their downstream use case
when selecting an algorithm.
The spatial structure underlying these metric differences is visible in the regime-
partitioning maps. Figure 7 shows the partitions produced by the four classical base-
lines on four representative datasets (Climate / Health / Hydrology / Politics). The
four classical baselines tend to produce more spatially fragmented partitions, particu-
larly in the politics and health domains. The corresponding regime maps for the six
K-Models family variants (and a fine-grained cross-variant breakdown) are provided in
Appendix F (Figure S4); they generate more spatially coherent regimes with clearer
boundaries, with GeoEvolve being the most coherent.

6. Discussion: Toward Autonomous Geospatial Algorithm Discovery
In this section we step back and interpret what the case study suggests about the
SEGA framework introduced in Section 3. Building on the structural description of
the discovered algorithm given in Section 5.1, Section 6.1 asks what general lessons can
be drawn from those refinements and how SEGA complements expert-driven design.
Section 6.5 outlines limitations and risks.
6.1. Insights and Complementarity with Expert-driven Design
Taken together, the case study supports a more general suggestion: when the opti-
mization objective for a geospatial problem can be specified in a computable form, SEGA
can be a useful complement to traditional, expert-driven algorithm development. In the
spatial regime case, the objective of reducing within-region structural variability while
increasing between-region differentiation was encoded as the bounded, ground-truth-
anchored Rand Index. Within this setting, the multi-agent system surfaced algorithmic
refinements (an internal search over the initial partition scale, connectivity-preserving
border refinement, spatially penalized reassignment) that align with established geo-
graphic intuitions and are useful starting points for further analysis. Table 5 outlines
26


--- Page 27 ---
several other geospatial problems for which optimization objectives can plausibly be
formalized and which may therefore benefit from a similar treatment.
Geospatial Problem

Table 5: Examples of geospatial problems with formalizable objectives that may be amenable to
SEGA-style algorithm discovery. In each case, the most demanding intellectual work remains the
formulation step.
SEGA is best understood as complementary to expert-driven design rather than a
replacement. Conceptual innovations from researchers, adding spatial weights to a re-
gression model, embedding contiguity constraints, introducing new estimators, continue
to mark out the design space and define what counts as a good answer; LLM-assisted
search then fills in parts of that space that are tedious to explore manually. The prac-
tical value of SEGA comes less from any single “intelligent” move and more from two
properties LLMs supply at low marginal cost: diversity (many candidate structural
modifications generated and tried within a short time window) and iteration speed
(each round of variation, evaluation, and selection completing in minutes rather than
weeks). The combination of an internal model-selection step over the initial partition
scale with a connectivity-guarded batch border refinement assembled in our evolved
2KModels is one such combination that no individual researcher would have necessarily
prioritized in advance, but that the search procedure surfaced by trying many alter-
natives. The implication for GIScience is that the bottleneck in geospatial algorithm
development is shifting from implementation effort toward specification effort: the ge-
ographer’s role takes on additional dimensions as a problem architect who defines the
objective landscape in which the LLM-driven search operates, while classical spatial
algorithms remain valuable both as seeds for evolution and as baselines that anchor
the comparison.
6.2. Shared Infrastructure: Benchmarks, Traces, and Validation
Making algorithm discovery a normal mode of geospatial research, rather than a
series of one-off demonstrations, requires shared infrastructure for evaluating what the
searches produce. The central object is a common benchmark: a fixed interface (in-
put/output signature), a fixed evaluation protocol in which metrics are computed by
the harness rather than by the candidate, and an explicit split between the instances a
search may optimize against and those reserved for reporting. Validation then happens
on that benchmark: evolved algorithms should be compared against human-designed
algorithms of the same class — not only against their own seed — reported as dis-
tributions over independent evolution runs rather than single trajectories, and finally
27


--- Page 28 ---
evaluated on data the search never touched.
Seed algorithms and injected domain
knowledge, by contrast, should not be standardized: they are the researcher’s contri-
bution, the analogue of a hypothesis, and different seeds and knowledge bases exploring
the same benchmark is precisely the diversity that makes shared evaluation informa-
tive. The remaining piece is a standard evolution-trace format, recording per round
the candidate program, its fitness, and the prompt or knowledge that produced it. Be-
yond reproducibility, traces make credit assignable — a discovery is jointly produced
by whoever contributed the seed, the knowledge corpus, and the objective and search
design — and they are research material in their own right: with a common format,
questions such as which prompting regimes produce structural innovation rather than
parameter tuning become empirical questions answerable across laboratories.
6.3. Beyond Single-Objective, Simulation-Friendly Tasks
Extending SEGA past single-objective tasks requires distinguishing two situations.
When several objectives must all be respected but no trade-off curve is needed (e.g., ac-
curacy alongside runtime), lightweight randomized scalarization suffices: recent LLM-
driven evolution systems define several fitness metrics and randomly select one per
generation (Li et al., 2026). When the trade-off curve itself is the object of interest —
within-region homogeneity against region-size balance, or accuracy against uncertainty-
interval width — the search must instead maintain a set of non-dominated alternatives,
via explicit non-dominated sorting (Deb et al., 2000) or a quality-diversity archive in-
dexed by the competing objectives (Mouret and Clune, 2015); the MAP-Elites feature
map already used here for (score, complexity) is a natural place for that substitution.
Characterizing which geospatial problems need a frontier rather than a compromise is,
to us, the most concrete piece of future work.
6.4. Toward Trustworthy and Responsible Self-Evolving GeoAI
Self-evolution sharpens a known ethical problem of spatial analysis. Chen et al.
(2026) show that endogenous bias arises whenever a global optimization goal diverges
from the local needs of particular regions or communities: the aggregate looks sound
while some places or groups are systematically disadvantaged. An evolutionary search
is an aggregate optimizer by construction, keeping any variant that raises mean fit-
ness, even one that concentrates errors in a few regions, and since no one designed
the evolved mechanism, such trade-offs are easily missed. Three checkpoints follow.
Before the search, the problem should be deliberately delimited, and where distri-
butional consequences matter, the objective should register them (e.g., worst-region
terms alongside the mean, Section 6.3) rather than average them away; our restric-
tion of regime discovery to descriptive partitioning (Section 4.1) is a modest instance.
Before deployment, the evolved algorithm should be diagnosed, not only scored: vi-
sual analytics (Chen et al., 2026) can map its errors and uncertainty, which are rarely
uniform over space and so translate into spatially uneven risk, and check the spatial
continuity of the parameters it estimates. At deployment, performance established
in one study region cannot be assumed to transfer, so local diagnostics, recalibra-
tion where needed, and disaggregation of results by spatial unit and population group
should precede any decision. However much of the search is delegated, the judgement
of whom its results serve remains the geographer’s.
28


--- Page 29 ---
6.5. Limitations and Risks
While the present results are encouraging, several limitations and risks deserve
attention. Dependence on objective-function quality. The hypothesis that prob-
lems with well-defined objectives can be partly addressed by autonomous search places
a heavy burden on the objective itself. Poorly specified loss functions may lead the
evolutionary system to favor algorithms that optimize the metric while drifting away
from the intended geographic phenomenon; the choice of RandI as the fitness signal
in our case study is a concrete instance of how carefully this choice must be made.
Problems with ill-defined objectives. Not all geospatial problems admit clean,
easily formalizable objectives. Tasks such as cartographic generalization, place char-
acterization, or qualitative spatial reasoning involve aesthetic, cognitive, or contextual
judgements that are difficult to reduce to a single scalar metric; for such problems,
hybrid approaches combining human judgement with autonomous search are likely to
be needed. Interpretability and trust. Evolved algorithms can be more difficult
to interpret than manually designed ones; the evolved 2KModels’ interacting heuris-
tics — a candidate-set search over initial cluster counts nested inside the two-stage
procedure, and a border-refinement stage whose penalty magnitude, iteration budget
and patience were tuned by the search rather than derived from theory — lack the
conceptual transparency of methods derived from first principles, which raises legiti-
mate concerns for scientific reproducibility. Knowledge-base bias. The geographic
knowledge base K inevitably reflects the choices, blind spots, and disciplinary tenden-
cies of its source materials; over-representing certain methodological traditions (e.g.,
spatial econometrics) while under-representing others (e.g., qualitative geography) can
steer the evolutionary search toward a narrow region of the solution space. Single
seed and task family.
All empirical evidence comes from one seed algorithm in
one task family: the case study demonstrates feasibility, not generality. Establishing
SEGA as a general paradigm requires demonstrations across algorithm families under
the same evaluation discipline; until then, framework-level statements should be read
as scoped to problems resembling the one studied here. Computational cost and
reproducibility. LLM-driven evolution requires substantial computational resources
and depends on language models whose behavior may change across versions, making
bit-for-bit reproducibility difficult.
7. Conclusion
This paper presented Self-Evolving Geospatial Algorithms (SEGA), a framework
for developing geospatial algorithms through a structured, evaluation-driven LLM-
assisted inner loop alongside the traditional expert-driven discovery carried out by
researchers. SEGA rests on three required modules: a two-loop architecture with em-
bedded geographic knowledge (adopted from GeoEvolve), an automatic code formatter
that turns any raw seed algorithm into the standardized input the inner loop requires,
and a simulation-driven training protocol that disciplines the use of data and metrics
so that real-world performance counts as out-of-sample evidence. The spatial regime
case study validates the full stack: the knowledge-guided evolved Two-stage K-Models
outperforms both its seed and knowledge-free baselines on 150 simulated grids, trans-
fers without retuning to 11 real-world datasets across climate, health, hydrology, and
politics, and remains competitive with four classical regionalization baselines on real
29


--- Page 30 ---
data. We close with a hypothesis that this case study supports but cannot yet estab-
lish: when a geospatial problem admits a computable optimization objective, much
of the inner-loop work of algorithm refinement may be delegable to LLM-driven sys-
tems; demonstrating this beyond a single seed and task family is the necessary next
step. What the study does show is the geographer’s contribution shifting upstream,
toward articulating new questions, designing meaningful loss functions, and building
trustworthy evaluation protocols.
8. Data and Code Availability
The complete code and data accompanying this paper, together with an interactive
trace of the evolution it reports, are available from the project page: https://peng-
luo.com/sega/.
