Appendix B. Configuration of GeoEvolve Used in the Case Study
This appendix records the runtime configuration used to evolve the spatial regime
algorithms reported in this paper, so that the case study can be reproduced without
consulting Luo et al. (2025). Settings not listed here are inherited from that system
paper without modification.
B.1 LLM backbone and evolutionary search
The framework is LLM-agnostic in principle; any chat-completions backbone may
be substituted via a single configuration entry. In this case study we used a weighted
pair of OpenAI models accessed through OpenRouter: openai/gpt-4o as the pri-
mary model (weight 0.8) and openai/gpt-4.1 as the secondary model (weight 0.2),
with sampling parameters temperature = 0.7, top_p = 0.95, and max_tokens = 8192.
The same backbone is used by all agents (Code Evolver, Code Analyzer, Knowledge
Retriever, and Geo-informed Prompt Generator).
The code evolver is OpenEvolve
(Sharma, 2025), which serves as the inner loop. Concretely, all GeoEvolve-based vari-
ants are run through the open-source Python package geoevolve, distributed alongside
Luo et al. (2025); the package handles the orchestration of the four agents and exposes
the configuration entries described below. The total evolutionary budget is held con-
stant at 100 iterations across all variants: for OpenEvolve-based variants this is a single
flat loop of 100 iterations; for GeoEvolve-based variants it is 10 outer-loop cycles, each
invoking the analyzer, retriever (when enabled), and prompt generator once, with 10
inner-loop iterations per cycle. The search uses a MAP-Elites population of 50 pro-
grams with archive size 20, organized into 5 islands, with elite/exploration/exploitation
selection ratios of (0.1, 0.2, 0.7) and a 10 × 10 (score, complexity) feature map. Each
evaluation is allowed up to 100 seconds and at most three retries.
B.2 Algorithm variants
Five variants are compared in addition to the unevolved seed: (i) OpenEvolve
(No GeoKnow.), the vanilla code-evolution loop with no domain-knowledge injection;
(ii) OpenEvolve (General GeoKnow.), a fixed natural-language hint about general
spatial-modeling concerns (Tobler’s first law, spatial autocorrelation, scale effects); (iii)
OpenEvolve (Specific GeoKnow.), a fixed hint additionally listing spatial-regime-
specific modifications such as contiguity penalties and region-size balancing; (iv) Geo-
Evolve (No GeoKnowRAG), the full multi-agent dialogue with the retrieval module
disabled; and (v) GeoEvolve, the complete pipeline with GeoKnowRAG enabled. The
prompt templates for (ii) and (iii) match those in Luo et al. (2025, Section 4).
B.3 GeoKnowRAG and code analyzer
The geospatial knowledge database is reused unchanged from Luo et al. (2025): 124
documents (75,228 chunks in the vector store, verified against the archived database
used for the reported runs) drawn from peer-reviewed publications, Wikipedia entries,
and open-source GitHub repositories, organized into five categories (geostatistics, spa-
tial theory, GIScience, spatial statistics, and spatial modeling). Representative key-
words span kriging theory, Tobler’s first law, spatial autocorrelation, the modifiable
areal unit problem, and spatial-interaction models. Chunks of 300 tokens (50-token
overlap) are embedded with text-embedding-3-large, stored in a Chroma vector
32


--- Page 33 ---
database, and retrieved with RAG-Fusion (reciprocal rank fusion over multi-angle
sub-queries).
The Code Analyzer is prompted to (i) identify missing or problem-
atic geographic knowledge, (ii) suggest up to three search queries for the retriever,
and (iii) flag whether code examples or theoretical background are needed; it re-
turns strict JSON with keys missing_or_problematic_knowledge, search_queries,
need_code_examples, and need_geographical_theory.
B.4 Task-specific settings for spatial regime discovery
The settings below differ from Luo et al. (2025) only because the case study ad-
dresses a different task. The seed algorithm A0 is Two-stage K-Models (Guo et al.,
2023) (Section 4.1). The simulator produces 150 grids of size 25 × 25 (Section 4.2.1),
evenly split across three latent regime patterns (Rectangular, Voronoi, Arbitrary) at
the high-noise level. The fitness signal is the Rand Index against the ground-truth
partition (Section 4.2.1); no SSR-family metric is used as a fitness signal. The target
number of regions is p = 5 on simulated data, and on real-world data p is inferred
from the dataset’s administrative-unit structure (Section 4.3.1). The spatial weights
matrix is a rook-contiguity matrix from libpysal.weights.lat2W on the 25×25 grid
for simulated data, and a row-standardized k-nearest-neighbor matrix with k = 6 for
real-world data. The minimum region size is 10 cells (simulated) and 10 observa-
tions (real-world). The evaluation metrics (SSR, SSR Reduction, RMSE, Variance
Ratio) are computed post-hoc by the evaluation harness and are never observed by Φ
during evolution; on real-world data they are model-fit statistics rather than predictive
scores, for the reasons set out in Section 4.3.1.
Appendix C. Computational Cost of the Case Study
This appendix reports what it cost to run the case study, separating two quantities
that are easily conflated: the cost of discovering an algorithm (the evolution loop)
and the cost of running the discovered algorithm (inference). Both are measured, not
estimated.
Token counts are recorded per API call by instrumenting the client SDK, so they
cover the inner evolution loop, the four GeoEvolve agents, and GeoKnowRAG retrieval
and embedding calls alike. We report token counts rather than monetary cost because
tokens are a property of the run, whereas prices depend on the provider and change
over time; a reader can convert to their own provider’s rates. (At the provider list
prices in effect in August 2026, the measured usage corresponds to roughly US$6–11
per 100-iteration run: US$5.5–6.4 for the GeoEvolve variants and US$10.3–11.3 for the
OpenEvolve variants.)
Elapsed time is measured from the start of an evolution run to the completion of
its final iteration, and inference time is the mean runtime of a discovered algorithm
per grid over the 150 grids. All timings were measured on one machine (Apple M5);
inference used six worker processes.
Three observations follow from Table C.5. First, a complete 100-iteration evolution
is inexpensive in absolute terms: under 4M tokens and roughly an hour of elapsed time
at most for every variant. Discovery cost is therefore not the binding constraint on this
kind of work; run-to-run variance is (Section 5.2).

Table C.5: Average measured computational cost per variant. Evolution columns refer to one 100-
iteration evolution run; Inference is the runtime of the discovered algorithm on one 625-cell grid. For
GeoEvolve (GeoKnowRAG) the inference column reports the mean ± SD over all three evolution runs,
followed in parentheses by the trimmed mean† that excludes the one run whose refinement step lacks
early stopping (tail behaviour described in the text); no other variant has any run excluded from any
column. Measurement conditions are described in the text.
Second, the GeoEvolve variants consume roughly half the input tokens of the
OpenEvolve variants (1.7–1.9M versus 3.7–4.0M) despite issuing about twice as many
API calls. The reason is structural rather than a property of retrieval: GeoEvolve
restarts the inner loop every ten iterations, so the program database — from which the
prompt draws its top-performing and diverse exemplars — is rebuilt each round and
supplies fewer exemplars in the early iterations of every round. A flat 100-iteration loop
instead accumulates a full archive and quickly saturates the prompt. Measured per-call
prompt length shows this directly: GeoEvolve prompts follow a sawtooth from ∼7k to-
kens at the start of each round to ∼40k by its end (median ∼22k), whereas OpenEvolve
prompts sit near ∼42k throughout. Disabling GeoKnowRAG leaves this profile essen-
tially unchanged (median 21.7k versus 21.8k with retrieval enabled), confirming that
the saving comes from the two-loop schedule and not from retrieval compression.
Third, inference cost varies far more across variants than discovery cost does, and
the ordering does not follow accuracy. The overhead of the GeoEvolve algorithm rel-
ative to the seed comes from two explicit and adjustable choices — the number of
candidate cluster counts searched in stage one, and the iteration budget and patience
of the border-refinement step — rather than from any fixed property of the framework.
One evolved program illustrates the risk of leaving those choices unconstrained: its re-
finement step has no early stopping, so although its median grid takes 4.8 s, it exceeds
ten minutes on 19 of the 150 grids, for a per-grid mean of 188.9 s. The missing early
stopping makes it slow, not unreliable: like every other frozen program, it completes
all 150 grids. This slow behaviour is itself an outcome of the discovery process, so
Table C.5 reports the inference cost of GeoEvolve (GeoKnowRAG) over all three runs,
with the clearly marked trimmed mean that excludes this run summarizing typical
behaviour rather than the tail. Evolution optimizes the fitness signal it is given, and
runtime was not part of that signal; a multi-objective fitness that prices runtime would
be a natural extension (Section 6).
Appendix D. Evolved Algorithm versus Seed under a Matched Budget, and
Component Ablations
Compared with its seed, the evolved algorithm spends more computation at infer-
ence: it searches six initial cluster counts and adds a border-refinement stage. This
34


--- Page 35 ---
appendix asks whether its advantage in Table 3 comes from that extra computation
or from its algorithmic content. Two analyses answer the question: a comparison with
the seed given the same search under a matched budget, and one-component ablations
of the evolved algorithm.
ARI, not SSR, is the comparison of record in this appendix. The reason
is structural. Because no ground-truth information may enter a candidate program
(Principle 4, Section 3.2.3), every selection rule available in this study — inside the
evolved algorithm and inside the matched-budget wrapper alike — must rank candidate
partitions by post-merge SSR. SSR is therefore the one quantity that additional search
can buy directly, and a search-based baseline will narrow the SSR gap whether or not it
has recovered any more of the regime structure. ARI, agreement with the ground-truth
partition, is reachable by no selection rule here, and it is the quantity spatial regime
discovery is defined on. Closeness on SSR between a search-based baseline and the
evolved algorithm is accordingly weak evidence of equivalence, and the two columns
are read separately below.
All variants are evaluated by the harness of Section 4.2.1 on the same 150 grids, in
a single batch on one machine. The reference row is the single frozen algorithm A⋆that
is carried forward to the real-world study, scored grid by grid; its figures are therefore
not the three-run means of Table 3, where the spread is across evolution runs rather
than across grids. Table D.6 reports the results; the programs, the runner, and the
per-grid results are in the project repository.
Evolved algorithm versus seed under a matched budget. This analysis tests whether
extra search alone reproduces the evolved algorithm’s advantage. The baseline is the
seed program, left unmodified, called by an external wrapper. The wrapper repeats
the seed’s partition-and-merge procedure over the same six initial cluster counts that
the evolved algorithm searches, {⌊2.5p⌋, 4p, ⌊√n⌋, p, p+1, p+2}, draws a fresh random
restart on each pass, and returns the run with the lowest post-merge SSR, which is the
label-free selection rule the evolved algorithm itself uses. It stops once it has used the
evolved algorithm’s mean per-grid runtime in the same batch (7.5 s). The remaining
asymmetries favour the baseline: it always completes at least one full pass over the
six counts, and it checks the budget only between runs, so it actually takes 1.11 times
as long as the evolved algorithm. The outcome divides along exactly the line drawn
above. On ARI, which no selection rule in this study can target, the gap persists in all
three spatial patterns: the evolved algorithm recovers the true regimes better (0.894
versus 0.854; median ∆ARI +0.043, p = 2.3×10−10), and the budgeted search recovers
only a little over half of the seed’s deficit (0.801 →0.854, against 0.801 →0.894 for the
evolved algorithm). On SSR, the quantity the wrapper selects on directly, additional
search closes most of the gap (seed 80.5, baseline 60.6, evolved 59.0), leaving a small
but significant margin (median ∆SSR −1.90, p = 2.1×10−5). Additional computation
therefore accounts for most of the SSR advantage but not for the recovery of the regime
structure itself, and the asymmetry between the two columns is what a baseline that
optimizes one of them and not the other should be expected to produce.
Component ablations. The ablations locate the advantage that remains, and they do
so in the direction opposite to what a parameter-search account of the gains would
predict. Each removes one component from the frozen evolved algorithm with a single
commented change: the initial-cluster-count search (replaced by the seed’s fixed count
35


--- Page 36 ---
of 20); border refinement (the stage that reassigns boundary units after merging); the
spatial penalty inside that stage (which discourages moving a unit into a region where
it has fewer neighbours); or KMeans++ initialization (replaced by the seed’s random
assignment).
The one component that is purely a matter of search effort, the initial-cluster-
count search, contributes the least of the three that contribute at all (median ∆SSR
−0.33, ∆ARI +0.004), while the structural addition contributes an order of magnitude
more (border refinement: median ∆SSR −7.09, ∆ARI +0.063, p < 10−24 on both).
KMeans++ initialization contributes nothing detectable (p = 0.68) while accounting
for 43% of the runtime — a component the search had no reason to prune, because
runtime was not part of the fitness signal (Appendix C). The spatial penalty is the
clearest case of all: it contributes +0.039 ARI even though removing it lowers SSR
(median ∆SSR +1.80, p = 3.9 × 10−19), trading fit for agreement with the true struc-
ture. Because its value is negative in the algorithm’s own selection objective, no tuning
of the seed’s parameters against that objective could have found it; it is a structural
contribution of the discovery process rather than a setting a grid search would have
reached.

ARI is the comparison of record: SSR is the quantity every selection rule in this study
optimizes directly (Principle 4), so closeness on SSR does not indicate equivalence. SSR
and ARI are mean ± SD over grids, computed externally by the harness.
∆SSR and ∆ARI are
per-grid medians of (evolved −variant), each with the p-value of a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test;
negative ∆SSR and positive ∆ARI favour the evolved algorithm. Paired medians are reported because
the per-grid SSR distribution is right-skewed, so they need not match the difference of the means in
the first column. Rel. time is each program’s mean per-grid runtime relative to the evolved algorithm
(= 1.00), all measured in the same batch. The two identical p-values in the last row arise from the
signed-rank statistic taking mirror-image values on the two metrics; they are a coincidence, not a
transcription error.
Appendix E. Worked Example of the Automatic Code Formatter on Two-
stage K-Models
This appendix traces what the automatic code formatter (Module 2 , Section 3.2.2)
did when applied to the Two-stage K-Models seed. The formatter’s job is to turn the
raw source into the standardized triple (Ainit, Eeval, Cconfig) introduced in Section 3.2.2,
plus a small metadata file. Figure S1 summarizes the end-to-end run; Sections Ap-
pendix E.1–Appendix E.3 below show the raw input, the three produced artifacts, and
a short narrative of the case-study-specific elements.
36

Figure S1: Trace of the automatic code formatter on the Two-stage K-Models seed. Three LLM chains
transform the raw .py input into the standardized triple plus a metadata file: initial_program.py
(Ainit), evaluator.py (Eeval), config.yaml (Cconfig), and _format_metadata.json.
Chain #1 is
followed by a deterministic syntactic check that parses the generated program with Python’s ast
module, locates the standardized run_algorithm entry function, and verifies that its body contains
at least one return statement returning a non-None value; when the check fails, an LLM-driven repair
step is invoked at most twice before the formatter falls back to the user. For this seed the check passed
on the first attempt.
Appendix E.1. Input: the raw Two-stage K-Models implementation
The raw input Araw was a single .py file containing our implementation of the
Two-stage K-Models algorithm of Guo et al. (2023).
The core of the file is the
two-stage entry point, reproduced in abbreviated form in Listing 1:
a first-stage
run_kmodels call that partitions the units into 20 sub-regions, followed by a second-
stage merge_stage that enforces spatial contiguity, removes regions below min_size,
and merges until exactly p regions remain. The file also contains the underlying helper
functions (init_zones, fit_equations, closest_equation, merge_small_regions,
greedy_merge_until_p, . . . )
and the data-loading / metric-computation utilities.
Crucially, the raw file does not declare which parts of the code should be considered
mutable by an evolutionary loop and does not expose a uniform entry point for an
external evaluator, those are the two responsibilities the formatter takes on.
Listing 1: Excerpt from the raw Two-stage K-Models source Araw given to the formatter (helper
functions and data-loading utilities elided).
import numpy as np
import libpysal
def run_two_stage_kmeans(
X, Y, p, w,
min_size=None, max_iter=1000,
init_stoc_step=True, verbose=False):
"""A two-step kmeans-like regionalization algorithm."""
if min_size is None:
min_size = X.shape[1]
# Stage 1: partition into 20 sub-regions
labels_partition = run_kmodels(
37


--- Page 38 ---
X, Y, n_regions=20, w=w,
min_size=min_size, max_iter=max_iter,
init_stoc_step=init_stoc_step, verbose=verbose)
# Stage 2: merge into p connected regions
labels_merged = merge_stage(
X, Y, labels_partition, w,
p=p, min_size=min_size, verbose=verbose)
return labels_merged
Appendix E.2. Output: the standardized triple
Appendix E.2.1. Initial program Ainit
The formatter wrapped the algorithmic core of Araw in a single # EVOLVE-BLOCK-START
/ # EVOLVE-BLOCK-END pair and appended a standardized entry function named run_algorithm
below the block. The function name is fixed by the formatter (it is the same name the
formatter uses for every seed, and the same name the AST-based validation step checks
for), so that the evaluator can always import the program and call run_algorithm()
without seed-specific code. The block contains the entire two-stage algorithm together
with all helper routines that depend on the regionalization logic; the entry function lives
outside the block so that the inner loop cannot mutate the interface that the evaluator
relies on. Listing 2 shows the boundaries of the resulting initial_program.py.
Listing 2:
Boundaries of the formatter-produced initial_program.py (Ainit).
The evolvable
block contains the partitioning loop, the merge stage, and all helper functions; the standardized
run_algorithm() entry function below the block is what the evaluator calls.
# EVOLVE-BLOCK-START
import time
import numpy as np
import libpysal
def run_two_stage_kmeans(X, Y, p, w, min_size=None,
max_iter=1000, init_stoc_step=True,
verbose=False):
... # algorithmic core
return labels_merged
def run_kmodels(...): ... # Stage 1 (partition)
def merge_stage(...): ... # Stage 2 (merge)
def init_zones(...): ... # initialization
def fit_equations(...): ... # per-region OLS
# ... other helpers ...
# EVOLVE-BLOCK-END
# --- standardized entry function (not mutated by the inner loop) ---
def run_algorithm():
"""Run Two-stage K-Models on every simulated grid and return
the mean of the five evaluator-facing metrics."""
base_path = ’.../synthetic’
data_ids = (5, 75, 149)
ssr_list, randi_list, nmi_list, mae_list, time_list = [],[],[],[],[]
for id_ in data_ids:
data_path = f’{base_path}/grid_{id_}h.txt’
ssr, randi, nmi, mae, used_time = run_georegime_once(data_path)
ssr_list.append(ssr); randi_list.append(randi)
nmi_list.append(nmi); mae_list.append(mae)
38


--- Page 39 ---
time_list.append(used_time)
return (np.mean(ssr_list), np.mean(randi_list),
np.mean(nmi_list), np.mean(mae_list),
np.mean(time_list))
Appendix E.2.2. Evaluator module Eeval
The formatter wrote a evaluator.py module whose evaluate(program_path) en-
try point dynamically loads Ainit with importlib, calls program.run_algorithm()
on the simulator under a 100-second wall-clock timeout, and returns a dictionary of
five metrics together with a combined_score field that is the single scalar actually
consumed by the inner loop. Listing 3 shows the body of evaluate(). The key design
choice visible in the listing is that combined_score is set to randi: the Rand Index
is what drives evolutionary selection, while SSR, NMI, MAE, and used_time are re-
turned and logged but never fed back as fitness. This is the code-level enforcement of
the fitness/evaluation separation prescribed by the training protocol of Section 3.2.3.
Listing 3: Body of the formatter-produced evaluator.py (Eeval). The combined_score field (last line
of the returned dict) is what the inner-loop engine uses for selection; all other metrics are logged but
do not influence the search.
def evaluate(program_path):
spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("program", program_path)
program = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
spec.loader.exec_module(program)
if not hasattr(program, "run_algorithm"):
print("Error: program lacks the expected entry function")
ssr, randi, nmi, mae, used_time = run_with_timeout(
program.run_algorithm,
timeout_seconds=100)
return {"ssr": ssr,
"randi": randi, # fitness signal (RandI vs ground truth)
"nmi": nmi,
"mae": mae,
"used_time": used_time,
"combined_score": randi} # drives evolutionary selection
Appendix E.2.3. Configuration file Cconfig
The formatter emitted a YAML configuration file with five blocks: general evo-
lution settings, LLM settings, prompt configuration, population/archive parameters
for OpenEvolve’s MAP-Elites database, and evaluator settings. The most case-study-
specific block is the prompt configuration, where the formatter inserted a domain-
specific system message instructing the LLM that the task is to improve a spatial
regime algorithm and that the optimization target is the Rand Index. Listing 4 shows
the relevant blocks (full file: 100 lines). The LLM-generated YAML initially contains
the literal placeholder "YOUR_API_KEY" for llm.api_key; the formatter then post-
processes the file to replace the placeholder with whichever of OPENROUTER_API_KEY,
OPENAI_API_KEY, GEMINI_API_KEY, GROQ_API_KEY, or ANTHROPIC_API_KEY is present
in the environment (resolved in that priority order), and to rewrite llm.api_base so it
matches the backend implied by the model name (e.g. OpenRouter, Gemini’s OpenAI-
compatible endpoint, or Groq). The injection happens at write time so that no secret
ever lives in the source tree or in version control.
39


--- Page 40 ---
Listing 4: Key blocks of the formatter-produced config.yaml (Cconfig). API keys are written to the
file at run time from an environment variable so that no secret enters version control.
# --- General evolution settings ---
max_iterations: 10 # inner-loop iterations per outer cycle; GeoEvolve runs 10
cycles for 100 total (Appendix B.1); for OpenEvolve-only variants this is
overridden to 100 to run a single flat loop
diff_based_evolution: true
max_code_length: 25000
# --- LLM configuration ---
llm:
primary_model: "openai/gpt-4o"
primary_model_weight: 0.8
secondary_model: "openai/gpt-4.1"
secondary_model_weight: 0.2
temperature: 0.7
top_p: 0.95
max_tokens: 8192
# --- Prompt configuration (task-specific) ---
prompt:
system_message: "You are an expert in GIS and an experienced
coder. Your task is to improve the Spatial Regime algorithm
in Python ... The target is to maximize Rand index (RandI)."
# --- Database (MAP-Elites + island model) ---
database:
population_size: 50
archive_size: 20
num_islands: 5
elite_selection_ratio: 0.1
exploration_ratio: 0.2
exploitation_ratio: 0.7
feature_dimensions: ["score", "complexity"]
feature_bins: 10
# --- Evaluator ---
evaluator:
timeout: 100
max_retries: 3
parallel_evaluations: 4
Appendix E.2.4. Run metadata _format_metadata.json
Alongside the standardized triple, the formatter writes a small JSON file with
the information needed to audit and reverse the formatting run after the fact. For
the Two-stage K-Models seed it contains six fields:
original_path (the absolute
path of the raw input), original_type ("file" or "directory"; "file" for this
seed), original_files (a map from each input filename to the SHA-256 hash of
its content), run_function_name (always "run_algorithm" in the current format-
ter), description (the natural-language algorithm description the user supplied when
invoking the formatter), and created_at (an ISO 8601 timestamp). This file is not con-
sumed by the inner-loop engine; it is read by the companion function restore_from_geoevolve(),
which uses original_path / original_type to decide whether to write a single file or
40


--- Page 41 ---
a folder and uses original_files to verify, via hash comparison, that the raw source
has not been modified since the formatter was run.
Appendix E.3. Narrative
Evolvable-block identification. The formatter identified a single evolvable region in Araw
and placed one # EVOLVE-BLOCK-START / # EVOLVE-BLOCK-END pair around it. The
region it chose corresponds to the partitioning loop, the merge stage, and all of their
helper routines, exactly the algorithmic locus that subsequent evolved variants ended
up modifying. The data-loading utility (input_data), the metric-computation class
(RegionMetrics), and the per-dataset driver (run_georegime_once) were correctly
kept outside the block, which is what made it safe for the evolved variants to mutate
the algorithm without breaking the evaluator-facing interface.
First-pass correctness of the evaluator. The evaluator generated by the second chain
ran successfully on the first attempt: it imported Ainit, found the standardized run_algorithm
entry function, called it under the 100-second timeout, and reported the five-metric dic-
tionary together with combined_score set to randi. The deterministic AST-based val-
idation step on run_algorithm (Figure S1) was therefore not triggered, and the LLM-
driven repair step was not invoked. The reverse operation, restore_from_geoevolve(),
was not used at this stage of the case study but is available for splicing an evolved
initial_program.py back into the user’s original file structure using the hashes and
paths recorded in _format_metadata.json.
Configuration choices. The configuration file was produced in one pass and reflects
the OpenEvolve defaults with one task-specific override: the system message embeds
the domain ("Spatial Regime algorithm") and the optimization target ("Rand index").
The MAP-Elites feature dimensions score and complexity were left at their defaults;
the LLM choice (GPT-4o as primary with GPT-4.1 as a secondary fallback) and the
temperature 0.7 were inherited from the formatter’s prompt template and not modified
per task.
Appendix F. Detailed K-Models Variant Comparison
This appendix provides the detailed within-family breakdown of the six Two-stage
K-Models variants on real-world data, complementing the main-text comparison of
GeoEvolve against the four classical regionalization baselines (Section 5.3) and the per-
pattern simulation breakdown already reported in Table 3. The real-world breakdown
spans all 11 datasets in four application domains: climate, health, hydrology, and
politics, and includes a fine-grained six-variant regime-map breakdown (Figure S4).
Real-world cross-domain bar chart: full ten-algorithm comparison. Figure S2 expands
the compact ten-algorithm SSR-Reduction summary in main-text Figure 6 and the
six-algorithm Table 4 into a per-dataset, four-metric breakdown across all 11 datasets,
additionally displaying the three OpenEvolve variants and GeoEvolve without Geo-
KnowRAG (which are absent from Table 4) so that readers can see the full within-
family detail of the K-Models seed and all its evolved variants alongside the four classi-
cal baselines. The patterns visible in this fuller chart are consistent with the main-text
summary: GeoEvolve is the most consistent winner on RMSE and SSR Reduction
41

across both the K-Models family and the classical baselines; AZP is the most compet-
itive classical baseline on R2; and the OpenEvolve variant with a general geographic-
knowledge prompt attains a high Variance Ratio (mean 0.487, five first-place wins out
of 11 datasets), although it does not match GeoEvolve on RMSE or SSR Reduction.

Sensitivity to the number of spatial regimes. Figure S3 examines the sensitivity of
algorithm performance to the prescribed number of spatial regimes (R), ranging from
3 to 12. SSR reduction and the variance ratio increase monotonically across all three
algorithms, while average RMSE decreases correspondingly, consistent with the greater
flexibility of finer spatial partitions. Across the considered range of R, GeoEvolve tends
to attain higher SSR reduction and variance ratio, and lower average RMSE. Notably,

at R = 8.

Figure S3: Sensitivity of algorithm performance to the number of spatial regimes. Each panel reports
the mean value (solid line) ± one standard deviation (shaded band) across 11 datasets for SSR

Spatial regime assignments across the six K-Models variants. Figure S4 reports the
regime maps for all six Two-stage K-Models variants on four representative datasets
(Climate / Health / Hydrology / Politics), complementing the classical-baseline maps
in main-text Figure 7.
The figure isolates the visual effect of each step along the
knowledge-injection design axis (no prompt →general prompt →specific prompt →
multi-agent dialogue without retrieval →full GeoKnowRAG). Several qualitative pat-
terns stand out across the four domains. In the climate domain, all variants produce a
similar macro-structure that separates the western arid/semi-arid zone from the more
humid east, and GeoEvolve tends to draw sharper boundaries along the Rocky Moun-
tain front. In the health domain (Cancer dataset as an example), the seed algorithm
tends to produce a single dominant region spanning the eastern United States, whereas
GeoEvolve yields a more balanced partition that distinguishes the Appalachian corri-
dor from the southeastern coastal plain. The hydrology domain shows the greatest
agreement across methods, reflecting the strong hydroclimatic zonation of the contigu-
ous United States. For politics, GeoEvolve delineates a sharper urban-corridor versus
rural-interior contrast, particularly along the Northeast–Mid-Atlantic megalopolis and
the Pacific coast.

Dominant covariate maps. Figure S5 maps the dominant covariate, defined as the pre-
dictor with the largest absolute standardized coefficient (arg max |β|) excluding the
intercept, for each observation. The seed algorithm produces relatively fragmented,
locally heterogeneous patterns; OpenEvolve introduces more spatial continuity with
partially consolidated regions; GeoEvolve produces more spatially coherent and re-
gionally structured regimes, with clearer clustering and smoother transitions between
dominant covariates. For health, hydrology, and politics, the leading drivers across the
three algorithms are similar (no exercise, precipitation, and the percentage of Black
residents, respectively); in the climate domain, the dominant covariate differs across
algorithms, with thermal radiation most prominent for the GeoEvolve-evolved version.

Spatially varying regression coefficients. Figure S6 illustrates the spatial variation of
one scientifically relevant regression coefficient per domain: solar radiation (β7) for cli-
mate, smoking rate (β5) for health, precipitation (β1) for hydrology, and the percentage
of bachelor’s degrees (β4) for politics. In the climate domain, the solar radiation co-
efficient is strongly positive in the western US, where solar insolation drives surface
temperature, and decreases eastward under the influence of cloud cover and humidity.
GeoEvolve produces sharper transitions near the 100th meridian, consistent with the
well-documented aridity boundary. The precipitation coefficient in the hydrology do-
main is strongly positive in high-runoff regimes (Pacific Northwest, Appalachian high-
lands) and weakly positive in arid regimes; this pattern is preserved across algorithms
but is more sharply drawn by GeoEvolve.
